prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "TotalEnergies SE" (ticker TTE), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TTE", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: TotalEnergies SE
result.industry: Integrated oil, gas, LNG and power
markets: Oil and gas exploration and production
Liquefied natural gas (LNG) production and trading
Fuel retail, lubricants and aviation fuels (Marketing & Services)

mission.statement: Our purpose is to provide as many people as possible with energy that is more affordable, more reliable and more sustainable.
mission.source: TotalEnergies company website (Company > Identity, 'TotalEnergies at a glance')
mission.plain: TotalEnergies wants to supply lots of people with energy that costs less, is dependable and is cleaner.

about.plain: TotalEnergies is a big French energy company. It pumps oil and natural gas out of the ground and from under the sea in dozens of countries. It cools gas into a liquid and ships it around the world, turns oil into petrol, diesel, jet fuel and plastics, and sells fuel at its own petrol stations. It also makes electricity from gas plants, solar farms and wind farms and sells it to homes and businesses.
about.customers: Drivers, airlines, factories, power companies, households buying electricity and gas, and whole countries that import gas.
about.everyday: Its red, orange and blue TotalEnergies petrol stations are common across France, Europe and Africa, and many French homes buy their electricity and gas from it.

money.plain: petrol, diesel, jet fuel and motor oil
fuels and plastics made in its refineries
crude oil and gas from Africa, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas
gas cooled to a liquid and shipped worldwide
power from gas, solar and wind plants sold to homes and firms

money.part: Flexible power in Europe (EPH joint venture)
money.plain: gas-fired power plants that back up wind and solar, added in April 2026

result.summary: TotalEnergies sells commodities at market prices, so it has little pricing power; its edge is a low-cost, diversified upstream portfolio, one of the three largest LNG businesses and an integrated value chain from gas field to electricity customer. Long-life stakes in Qatar, the UAE, Mozambique, Uganda, Suriname and Namibia and a growing power business (48.1 TWh in 2025, targeted at 100-120 TWh by 2030) give it a narrow but real moat in a cyclical industry.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenues from sales track oil and gas prices it does not set: $119,704M in 2020, $263,310M in 2022, down to $182,344M in 2025, then up 15.2% to $106,613M in 1H 2026 as Brent averaged $92.3/b during the Middle East conflict, even though Middle East shut-ins cut Q2 2026 production by about 210 kboe/d.

moats.evidence: The TotalEnergies retail and lubricants brand (Quartz) is strong in France and Africa, but fuels, gas and electricity are bought mainly on price, and the 2021 rebrand from Total has not created a meaningful price premium.
Drivers and most industrial buyers switch suppliers freely; only long-term LNG sale contracts, power purchase agreements and fleet fuel-card contracts lock customers in for years.
A larger LNG and power portfolio gives trading flexibility, but more customers do not make the product more valuable to other customers.
It produced 2,529 kboe/d in 2025, sold 43.9 Mt of LNG and earned a 12.6% ROACE (13.9% for the twelve months to June 2026), helped by large, long-life fields in Qatar, the UAE and Brazil.

LNG plants and deepwater developments such as Mozambique LNG, Papua LNG and Suriname's GranMorgu cost billions of dollars and take years to build, which limits how many players can take part in each project.

Its integrated power strategy (targeting 100-120 TWh by 2030 and positive Integrated Power free cash flow in 2027) differs from US majors that avoid power, but European peers Shell and BP pursued the same model before retreating, so it is not a model rivals cannot copy.

Decades of operating experience in Africa, the Middle East and deepwater, together with an integrated gas, LNG, power and trading organisation, are hard to replicate quickly, although every supermajor has similar engineering depth.

Long-life stakes in Qatar's North Field LNG expansions, Abu Dhabi concessions, Uganda's Tilenga field, Suriname and Namibia's Venus discovery are scarce assets, though they are shared with partners and host governments.

customers.evidence: It has large retail and electricity customer bases in France and Europe and long-term LNG buyers in Asia, but most of its fuel, gas and chemicals are bought on price under commodity contracts, so loyalty is limited.

talent.evidence: It remains a sought-after employer for French engineers and geoscientists, but in the 2026 Universum survey of French engineering students Thales was named preferred employer for the second year running, and oil companies' appeal to young graduates has weakened over climate concerns.

product.evidence: Its upstream portfolio and LNG trading are considered among the best of the majors on cost and returns, but crude oil, gas, electricity and most refined products are interchangeable commodities.

threats: Oil and gas price swings: 2026 profits were lifted by the Middle East conflict (Brent averaged $103.8/b in Q2 2026), which could reverse as prices normalise.

Middle East exposure: Qatar LNG shut-ins and regional production losses averaged 210 kboe/d in Q2 2026 and were expected at 5-10% of output in Q3 2026; routes through the Strait of Hormuz remain at risk.
A wave of new LNG supply later this decade could squeeze LNG prices and trading margins.
Execution and security risks on large frontier projects such as Mozambique LNG, Uganda's Tilenga/EACOP and Suriname's GranMorgu.
The power strategy may earn lower returns than oil and gas (Integrated Power only targets a 12% ROACE by 2030), and long-term oil demand could decline with electric vehicles and climate policy.
Litigation and activist pressure over climate and human rights, including cases in France under the duty-of-vigilance law.

ceo.name: Patrick Pouyanné
ceo.background: Engineer, École Polytechnique and Corps des Mines; former French government adviser; joined Total in 1997, CEO since October 2014 and Chairman since 2015

c1.evidence: Oil and gas is a mature industry; its fast-growing power business (48.1 TWh in 2025) is small next to utilities, so it is not the leader of an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Partners and host governments pick it for its low-cost operating record and LNG and Africa expertise (e.g. Qatar North Field, Uganda, Suriname), but end customers buy commodity products on price, so the edge is in access to resources rather than customer preference.

c3.evidence: The name is widely known in France, Europe and Africa through its petrol stations, but it is not the default leader of its industry the way ExxonMobil or Shell are seen, and few customers 'recommend' a fuel supplier.

c4.evidence: It repeats its purpose of energy that is 'more affordable, more reliable and more sustainable' and its multi-energy strategy, but management is openly focused on cash flow and shareholder returns, as the September 2026 dividend policy shows.

c6.evidence: “big oil, French, profitable, polluting” — the impression is mixed: investors see a well-run, high-dividend major, while much of the public associates it with climate damage and controversial projects such as EACOP in Uganda.

c7.evidence: Global energy demand is huge and growing, and electricity and LNG are secular growth areas, but its oil revenues ride a mature, cyclical market rather than a fast secular trend.

c8.evidence: The rename to TotalEnergies in 2021 signalled expansion into electricity, which it plans to grow to 100-120 TWh by 2030, but these remain extensions of an energy company rather than new markets of a different kind.

m1.evidence: Pouyanné has a clear, consistently stated picture of a 'multi-energy' company balancing LNG growth and electricity, but it is an incremental strategy rather than a visionary reinvention.

m2.evidence: As CEO since 2014 he thinks long term (projects out to 2035 in the September 2026 strategy) and is seen as very hands-on and hard-working, but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no clear evidence either way that Pouyanné leads mainly by serving employees and customers; his reputation is that of a demanding, top-down leader.

m5.evidence: He built a distinctive integrated-power business and kept investing in solar, wind and batteries, but TotalEnergies' culture is engineering- and execution-focused rather than one of constant product invention.

m6.evidence: Pouyanné is a Polytechnique and Corps des Mines engineer who ran exploration and production and refining before becoming CEO, and he presents operational and project details himself.

m7.evidence: He champions affordable energy access and emissions cuts (e.g. an 80% methane reduction target by 2030 versus 2020), but critics say continued fossil fuel growth and projects such as EACOP put profit ahead of the climate.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Pouyanné giving a commencement speech at a top university such as Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Pouyanné is known for blunt, outspoken comments on energy policy and climate activists, but he is not a cultural figure on the level of Elon Musk.

m9.evidence: Under Pouyanné, production rose to 2,529 kboe/d in 2025, ROACE was 12.6% in 2025, diluted EPS grew from $2.51 in 2015 to $5.78 in 2025, and the share count fell from 2,647M in 2021 to 2,214M in 2025.

m10.evidence: TotalEnergies is known for cost discipline in operations but not for a distinctive culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: Its fuel, gas and electricity power daily life for very many people across Europe, Africa and Asia, but these are commodities that many other suppliers also provide.

p2.evidence: Building deepwater fields, LNG plants and long pipelines such as Mozambique LNG and EACOP takes billions of dollars and rare engineering skill, and the energy is essential to the world economy.

f1.evidence: Revenues from sales rose from $119,704M (2020) to $263,310M (2022) but fell every year after, to $218,945M (2023), $195,610M (2024) and $182,344M (2025).

f2.evidence: It does not report gross or operating margin; net margin went from a loss in 2020 to 7.8% in 2022 and 7.2% in 2025 (net income $13,127M on $182,344M), with no steady rise.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at $130,953M and net debt is moderate at $19,710M (gearing 13.1%) at June 30, 2026, but gross debt of $62,708M exceeds cash and current financial assets of $31,717M.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow went from $14,803M (2020) to a peak of $47,367M (2022) and then fell to $27,343M (2025); net income followed the same up-then-down path.

v1.evidence: Its fuels, gas and electricity are commodities; there is no practical reason an ordinary person would choose TotalEnergies over Shell, BP or a local utility except price or location.

v2.evidence: It remains a well-regarded employer among French engineers, but it is not top-ranked: Thales was named the preferred employer of young French engineers in Universum's 2026 survey.

c5.evidence: Drivers, airlines, factories and gas-importing countries in Europe, Africa and Asia would feel an immediate supply shock if it disappeared, though other producers would eventually fill the gap, and its fossil fuels also add to climate change.
